title: pH Sets an Amino Acid's Charge

scenes.visual: Three cards (structure, charge, behavior) appear as the acts are named; R-group chip fills card 1, +/- tokens card 2, folding/binding/catalysis chips card 3, arrows link them; final numbered pulse 1-2-3.
scenes.narration: Every amino acid story has three acts—structure, charge, and behavior. This roadmap shows how an amino acid's backbone and R group shape its charge at physiological pH, and how structure and charge influence what it does—folding, binding, catalysis. Keep this sequence in mind—structure first, charge second, function third.

scenes.visual: pH strip with a yellow marker drives an amino acid shown as amino chip / R / carboxyl chip; chips change protonation state at the real pKa thresholds (2.3, 9.6) while a net-charge readout goes +1, 0, -1; the middle zone is shaded gold and labelled pI.
scenes.narration: At physiological pH, free amino acids have oppositely charged amino and carboxyl groups. Their charges cancel unless the side chain adds a charge. Drop the pH and the carboxylate gets protonated; raise it and the amino group loses its proton. The zwitterion dominates between those pKas, and at the isoelectric point, or pI, the average net charge is zero.

scenes.visual: A working seesaw with pH and pKa weights tips by their difference; a proton token on a group chip leaves when pH is above pKa and returns when below; rule lines written in sync; three consumers (titration curve, buffer, charged side chain) point back at the seesaw.
scenes.narration: Let's pin down the rule you'll use for the rest of biochemistry. It's a seesaw between pH and pKa. When the pH is greater than the pKa, the group gives up its proton. It's deprotonated. When the pH is less than the pKa, the group holds on. It's protonated. That's the whole rule. pH above pKa, proton off. pH below pKa, proton on. Drill it until it's automatic, because every titration curve, every buffer, and every charged side chain you meet from here on comes back to this one comparison.

scenes.visual: Burette dripping base into a beaker with pH readout, three step chips, and a live-plotted titration curve computed from two Henderson-Hasselbalch equilibria (pKa 2.34 / 9.60); plateaus shaded, pKa read at half-equivalence, pI marked at the midpoint with net charge 0.
scenes.narration: Titration is a three-step experiment. You add acid or base from a burette, monitor the pH in real time, and plot the resulting curve. What the curve reveals is remarkably informative. Each plateau's center gives a pKa. For glycine, shown here, the average of its two pKas gives the isoelectric point, where the average net charge is zero.

scenes.visual: Histidine charge ladder +2, +1, 0, -1 with pKa steps between rungs; the net-zero rung is highlighted, the two bracketing pKa values (6.0, 9.2) are averaged to pI = 7.6.
scenes.narration: When an amino acid has an ionizable side chain, finding its isoelectric point follows a simple shortcut. First, draw a charge ladder. Listing all protonation states from most positive at the top to most negative at the bottom, locate the net-zero zwitterionic form. The pI is simply the average of the two pKa values that bracket that neutral species. Find the neutral form first, then average the pKa values on either side.

scenes.visual: Fraction-protonated curve of the histidine side chain vs pH (pKa 6.0) with a pH 7.4 marker; a molecular switch flips between neutral and protonated, then three roles appear (active sites, metal coordination, pH sensing), knob finally rests half-way.
scenes.narration: Histidine's side-chain pKa is roughly 6.0 in free solution; protein environments can shift it. At pH 7.4, its side chain is mostly neutral, though some is protonated. This chemistry makes histidine useful in enzyme active sites, metal coordination, and pH sensing. Think of it as a molecular switch whose balance depends on its surroundings, ready to donate or accept a proton.
